student_passage:
Our science club wanted to offer a short activity during the school open day. We had no money for a large model, so we decided to create an imaginary night sky with a cardboard box and a torch. It would not be a real star map. Visitors would follow a story about a traveller looking for a way home.

(1) ____ The library had large windows, and the hall lights could not be switched off during the event. Finally, a music teacher offered us a practice room with thick curtains. We tried the box there after school, using a torch we already had. Once the curtains were closed, we could begin testing the effect.

We covered one side of the box with black paper and made holes of different sizes in it. (2) ____ When we turned the box, they moved slowly across it. This gave our traveller a sky to explore. A classmate wanted to add more and more holes, but too many points made it hard for the audience to follow the path described in the story.

We also discovered that some visitors would have only a few minutes, while younger children might want to stay longer and ask questions. (3) ____ One lasted three minutes; the other included pauses in which children could suggest where the traveller should go next. Both used exactly the same box and light.

On open day, the longer version became especially popular. Visitors disagreed about which pattern looked like a boat or a bridge, and their ideas changed the story each time. (4) ____ That became our test for any further changes to the activity: would they give visitors another way to join in?

filled_passage:
Our science club wanted to offer a short activity during the school open day. We had no money for a large model, so we decided to create an imaginary night sky with a cardboard box and a torch. It would not be a real star map. Visitors would follow a story about a traveller looking for a way home.

(1) Our first problem was simply finding a room dark enough. The library had large windows, and the hall lights could not be switched off during the event. Finally, a music teacher offered us a practice room with thick curtains. We tried the box there after school, using a torch we already had. Once the curtains were closed, we could begin testing the effect.

We covered one side of the box with black paper and made holes of different sizes in it. (2) The tiny holes produced points of light on the ceiling. When we turned the box, they moved slowly across it. This gave our traveller a sky to explore. A classmate wanted to add more and more holes, but too many points made it hard for the audience to follow the path described in the story.

We also discovered that some visitors would have only a few minutes, while younger children might want to stay longer and ask questions. (3) We therefore made two versions of the narration. One lasted three minutes; the other included pauses in which children could suggest where the traveller should go next. Both used exactly the same box and light.

On open day, the longer version became especially popular. Visitors disagreed about which pattern looked like a boat or a bridge, and their ideas changed the story each time. (4) Keeping the audience involved mattered more than copying the night sky perfectly. That became our test for any further changes to the activity: would they give visitors another way to join in?
